quests.instruction: A British colleague mentions that the team hasn't had a single customer complaint all month — then reaches over and raps her knuckles on the wooden desk. Which idiom does this describe?
quests.hint: It's a superstitious habit people add after mentioning good luck, hoping not to jinx it.
quests.explanation: 'Touch wood' (or 'knock on wood' in American English) is said after mentioning good fortune, as a superstitious way to avoid jinxing it. "We've never missed a deadline — touch wood."
quests.origin: Linked to old folk beliefs about spirits living in trees, who could be appealed to for protection by touching wood — though the precise origin is uncertain.

quests.instruction: Complete the phrase naturally: "Honestly, ___, I think the whole rebrand is a waste of money."
quests.hint: It's a phrase used right before confiding something private or a little indiscreet.
quests.explanation: 'Between you and me' signals a confidential, informal admission — the kind of thing said quietly to a trusted coworker or friend, not announced publicly. "Between you and me, I don't think this plan will work."
quests.origin: This question checks register awareness: recognizing when a phrase signals private, informal speech rather than formal or public communication.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: someone gently offering an opinion they're not fully confident will be valued.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: A humble way to introduce an opinion, signaling you're not sure how much it will matter.
quests.explanation: 'For what it's worth' is used to introduce an opinion modestly, acknowledging it may not carry much weight. "For what it's worth, I think the blue version looks better."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase questioning the value ('worth') of what follows, used as a polite hedge before giving an opinion.

quests.instruction: Which situation fits using this phrase naturally?
quests.hint: It's used casually, usually mid-conversation, right before condensing a longer account.
options: A CASUAL TEXT MESSAGE SUMMARIZING A CRAZY WEEKEND
OPENING LINE OF A FORMAL ACADEMIC ESSAY
THE FIRST LINE OF A LEGAL CONTRACT
quests.explanation: 'Long story short' is casual and conversational, typically used to skip ahead to the outcome of an anecdote. "Long story short, we missed the train and had to stay an extra night."
quests.origin: A shortened, more casual form of 'to make a long story short,' common in spoken and informal written English.

quests.instruction: A friend wants to criticize your new haircut without sounding harsh, so she softens it with a quick warning first: "Honestly, ___, I really don't think that style suits you."
quests.hint: It's a phrase people add right before saying something that might upset the listener.
quests.explanation: 'No offense, but' is used to soften criticism or a blunt opinion, signaling the speaker doesn't mean to be hurtful even though what follows might sting. "No offense, but I think we should redo the whole slide."
quests.origin: A common conversational hedge, functioning as a polite warning that a potentially unwelcome comment is coming next.

quests.word: AT THE END OF THE DAY
quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: someone wrapping up an argument by pointing to the one thing that ultimately matters most.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Used to introduce the most important conclusion after considering everything else.
options: AT THE END OF THE DAY
quests.explanation: 'At the end of the day' introduces the final, most important point after weighing everything else. "At the end of the day, what matters most is that the client is happy."
quests.correctAnswer: AT THE END OF THE DAY
quests.origin: A transparent metaphor treating a decision process like a day that eventually reaches its close, at which point the outcome is clear.

quests.instruction: A coworker says this after a project gets cancelled for reasons outside anyone's control. What tone does the phrase carry?
quests.hint: It's usually said with a mix of resignation and calm acceptance, not anger.
options: CALM ACCEPTANCE OF SOMETHING THAT CAN'T BE CHANGED
quests.explanation: 'It is what it is' expresses calm acceptance of an unchangeable situation, often with a hint of resignation. "The flight got cancelled — it is what it is, we'll rebook tomorrow."
quests.origin: A modern, widely used colloquial phrase that became especially common in casual English from the 1990s onward.

quests.instruction: Friend: 'I still think pineapple belongs on pizza.' You: '___, honestly, to each their own.'
quests.hint: It's a casual, easygoing way of saying someone's personal preference is fine, even if you don't share it.
options: AT THE END OF THE DAY
quests.explanation: 'Whatever floats your boat' means whatever makes someone happy or works for them is fine, even if it's not to your own taste. "You want to eat cereal for dinner? Whatever floats your boat."
quests.origin: A playful nautical image: whatever keeps a person's boat afloat and moving is acceptable, regardless of how unusual it looks to others.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: a slightly indifferent, mildly annoyed response to someone rejecting your suggestion.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: A somewhat clipped way of saying someone can do what they want, often with a hint of not fully agreeing.
options: AT THE END OF THE DAY
quests.explanation: 'Suit yourself' means someone can do as they wish, often said with a slight edge of indifference or mild disapproval. "You don't want to come? Suit yourself."
quests.origin: A plain, transparent phrase — literally telling someone to do what suits, or fits, their own preference.

quests.instruction: In which setting would this phrase most naturally be used?
quests.hint: It's a formal, polite way to soften disagreement, especially with someone in authority.
options: POLITELY DISAGREEING WITH A SENIOR EXECUTIVE IN A MEETING
TEXTING A CLOSE FRIEND ABOUT WEEKEND PLANS
quests.explanation: 'With all due respect' is a formal, polite way to introduce disagreement, especially toward someone senior or in authority. "With all due respect, I think that timeline is unrealistic."
quests.origin: A traditional, formal courtesy phrase used in English since at least the 1800s to soften direct disagreement.

quests.instruction: Manager: 'How did the presentation go?' Employee: '___, I think I rushed the ending a bit.'
quests.hint: It signals the speaker is about to give a candid, slightly vulnerable opinion, often self-critical.
quests.explanation: 'If I'm being honest' signals that the speaker is about to share a candid, sometimes uncomfortable opinion. "If I'm being honest, I don't think the design is finished yet."
quests.origin: A transparent conversational hedge that flags the coming statement as unusually direct or self-critical.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: someone about to say something potentially blunt, trying to soften it in advance.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: A hedge phrase used right before saying something that could come across as impolite.
quests.explanation: 'Not to be rude, but' is a hedge used before a potentially blunt or critical comment, to soften its impact. "Not to be rude, but that meeting could have been an email."
quests.origin: A common spoken-English cushioning device, part of a family of polite hedges including 'no offense' and 'with all due respect.'

quests.instruction: A mover carefully guiding a heavy piano down the stairs says this to his partner. What is he communicating?
quests.hint: It's said to encourage careful, slow, gentle action, especially in physical tasks.
options: GO SLOWLY AND CAREFULLY, DON'T RUSH
quests.explanation: 'Easy does it' is said to encourage slow, careful action, especially to avoid a mistake or accident. "Easy does it — that box has glass in it."
quests.origin: A simple imperative phrase, treating 'ease' or gentleness as the method ('does it') that gets the job done safely.

quests.instruction: A ship's captain uses this phrase during calm sailing conditions. In everyday speech, what would this most naturally encourage?
quests.hint: It's a nautical command that got adopted into general speech for staying steady and consistent.
quests.explanation: 'Steady as she goes' means to continue at a steady, consistent pace without sudden changes. "The project is on track — steady as she goes."
quests.origin: A genuine nautical helm command, instructing a ship to maintain its current, steady course.

quests.word: SLOW AND STEADY WINS THE RACE
quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: encouraging someone to trust a careful, consistent approach over rushing.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: A proverb encouraging patient, consistent effort rather than reckless speed.
options: SLOW AND STEADY WINS THE RACE
quests.explanation: 'Slow and steady wins the race' encourages patient, consistent effort over rushing. "Don't burn out — slow and steady wins the race."
quests.correctAnswer: SLOW AND STEADY WINS THE RACE
quests.origin: Drawn from Aesop's fable of the tortoise and the hare, where the slower but steadier tortoise wins the race.

quests.instruction: A friend describes their stressful first year of parenthood. What would this reply signal?
quests.hint: It's a casual way of showing you've personally experienced the same thing already.
options: INTEREST IN HEARING MORE DETAILS FOR THE FIRST TIME
SHARED PERSONAL EXPERIENCE WITH THE SAME SITUATION
quests.explanation: 'Been there, done that' means the speaker has already experienced the same thing personally. "Sleepless nights with a newborn? Been there, done that."
quests.origin: A casual, modern colloquial phrase that became especially common in English from the late 20th century onward.

quests.instruction: Coworker: 'I'm honestly dreading this client call.' You: '___.'
quests.hint: It's a quick, casual way of saying you feel exactly the same way.
quests.explanation: 'That makes two of us' means the speaker shares the same feeling or situation. "You're exhausted? That makes two of us."
quests.origin: A transparent, arithmetic-style phrase: if you feel that way, and I do too, that makes 'two' people who agree.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: a casual, slightly exasperated way of agreeing that something is frustrating, based on personal experience.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: An informal way to agree strongly, especially about something annoying or difficult, usually said sarcastically rather than as a literal request.
quests.explanation: 'Tell me about it' is used ironically to agree strongly, not as a literal request for information. "Traffic today was insane." "Tell me about it — I was stuck for an hour."
quests.origin: A conversational idiom where the literal words ('tell me') take on a sarcastic, non-literal meaning through tone.

quests.instruction: A manager wants to remind the team of a policy so obvious that stating it feels almost unnecessary, but she mentions it anyway: "___ that client data must stay confidential."
quests.hint: It introduces something considered so obvious that stating it feels almost unnecessary.
quests.explanation: 'Goes without saying' introduces a point considered obvious or already understood. "It goes without saying that we'll need everyone's input on this."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase noting that something is so clear it technically doesn't need to be spoken aloud, though it's said anyway for emphasis.

quests.instruction: ___, the client was furious when the shipment arrived three weeks late.
quests.hint: Like the previous idiom, it introduces something so predictable it barely needs stating.
quests.explanation: 'Needless to say' introduces a statement whose truth is obvious given the context. "Needless to say, we switched suppliers after that."
quests.origin: A close cousin of 'goes without saying,' both flagging an upcoming point as self-evident given what's already been said.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: a firm, serious way of emphasizing that a statement is absolutely certain, often used to prevent misunderstanding.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Used to stress that a statement should be taken very seriously and not doubted.
quests.explanation: 'Make no mistake' emphasizes that a statement is certain and shouldn't be doubted or misunderstood. "Make no mistake, this decision was not easy for the board."
quests.origin: A firm, formal phrase warning the listener not to misread or underestimate what follows.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "___, the renovation should cost around fifteen thousand dollars, though the exact number depends on the materials."
quests.hint: It introduces a general, rounded estimate at the start of a statement, rather than attaching to one specific figure.
quests.explanation: 'Roughly speaking' introduces an approximate statement, often at the start of a sentence. "Roughly speaking, we're looking at a six-month timeline."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase using 'roughly' in its sense of 'approximately,' paired with 'speaking' to frame the whole statement as an estimate.

quests.instruction: A colleague asks for a quick budget estimate. Which phrase more naturally attaches right after a specific number, rather than opening a general estimate?
quests.hint: One idiom typically follows a specific figure directly; the other more often introduces a general, rounded statement.
quests.explanation: 'Give or take' typically attaches directly after a specific number to show it's approximate, while 'roughly speaking' more often introduces a general estimate at the start of a sentence. "It'll cost about two thousand dollars, give or take."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'give or take.' This question checks awareness of natural word order and register, not just meaning.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Approximately, or almost completely, without being perfectly exact.
quests.explanation: 'More or less' means approximately or almost entirely. "The report is more or less finished — just a few edits left."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase pairing two opposite directions ('more,' 'less') to express a rough middle estimate.

quests.instruction: Which setting fits this phrase naturally?
quests.hint: It introduces a personal opinion, often signaling the speaker doesn't necessarily expect others to agree.
options: A FORMAL LEGAL DOCUMENT STATING FACTS
SOMEONE GIVING THEIR PERSONAL OPINION IN A DISCUSSION
quests.explanation: 'As far as I'm concerned' introduces a personal opinion, often implying the speaker's view may differ from others'. "As far as I'm concerned, the project was a success."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase limiting a statement to the speaker's own perspective or area of concern.

quests.instruction: ___, the whole meeting could have been a single email.
quests.hint: It's a casual way to offer an unsolicited personal opinion.
quests.explanation: 'If you ask me' introduces a personal opinion, often one that wasn't specifically requested. "If you ask me, the new logo is a big improvement."
quests.origin: A casual conversational phrase framing an opinion as a direct, honest answer, even when no one explicitly asked for it.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: someone offering their opinion while acknowledging it's shaped by their specific position or perspective.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: A phrase that introduces an opinion while acknowledging it's based on your own limited viewpoint.
quests.explanation: 'From where I'm standing' introduces an opinion while acknowledging it reflects a particular viewpoint or limited perspective. "From where I'm standing, the new policy seems unfair to part-time staff."
quests.origin: A literal spatial metaphor: what you can see, and therefore judge, depends on where you happen to be standing.

quests.instruction: After a competitive game, the losing team's captain shakes hands and says this. What is he communicating?
quests.hint: It's said to reassure someone that a past conflict or loss hasn't caused lasting resentment.
options: REASSURANCE THAT THERE'S NO RESENTMENT DESPITE THE OUTCOME
quests.explanation: 'No hard feelings' reassures someone that a disagreement or loss hasn't caused lasting resentment. "You got the promotion instead of me — no hard feelings, you earned it."
quests.origin: A plain, transparent phrase using 'hard feelings' as an old expression for bitterness or resentment.

quests.instruction: Roommate A wants total silence at night; Roommate B likes background music. After some tension, they agree to just ___ and respect each other's habits.
quests.hint: It's a philosophy of tolerating other people's different choices without judgment.
quests.explanation: 'Live and let live' means to tolerate other people's choices and lifestyles without judgment. "They don't share my taste in music, but live and let live."
quests.origin: A long-standing English proverb, recorded since at least the 1600s, expressing tolerance toward others' differences.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that fits this tone: two people ending a debate calmly, accepting that neither will change the other's mind.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Decide to accept differing opinions and stop arguing, without either side conceding.
quests.explanation: 'Agree to disagree' means to accept that two people won't reach the same conclusion and stop arguing about it. "We'll just have to agree to disagree on politics."
quests.origin: A transparent, self-explanatory phrase in use in English since at least the 1700s, used to formally end unresolved debates.
